company.name: OffloadCrew
company.tagline: You run the jobs. We'll run the office.
company.positioning: Back-office staffing for general contractors. Construction-trained, English-fluent remote assistants who work in the client's own email, phone line and software.
promises: No upfront cost and no recruiting or placement fee; the client pays nothing until they have met their assistant and said yes
A hand-picked assistant within about a week of the first call; most GCs are working with them within two weeks
Every placement starts with a 2-week trial; cancel during it and pay only the prorated time worked, refunded within 10 business days
Onboarding is handled by Offload Crew: access and the first handoffs are set up so the assistant is useful from week one
The client owns every account and can revoke access at any time; every assistant signs a confidentiality agreement

terms.billing: Monthly in advance, card or ACH
terms.replacement: At Offload Crew's discretion; credit for days without coverage when the assistant is unavailable on Offload's side

primer.why: Claims travel up the chain. If a sub's worker is injured or a sub damages the building, the GC and often the owner are pulled in, so the owner's contract requires the GC to prove every sub is insured. No valid COI generally means the sub should not be on site, and many GCs hold payment until one is on file. A lien waiver protects the owner from paying twice: a sub who is not paid can file a mechanic's lien on the property, so owners and lenders will not release payment without waivers from everyone on the job.
terms: ACORD 25: the standard one-page certificate of insurance. A summary, not the policy.

Coverages a GC typically requires: general liability, workers' comp, commercial auto, umbrella or excess on larger jobs, professional liability only for design-build trades. Limits come from the contract.
Additional insured: the GC is added to the sub's policy. It needs an endorsement, not just a name typed on the form.
Certificate holder: who the certificate is issued to. It gives no rights under the policy.
Waiver of subrogation, and primary and non-contributory: often required by contract; check that each is ticked.
A certificate is only good until the earliest expiration date on it.
W-9: the IRS form with the sub's legal name and taxpayer ID, needed before anyone is paid because the GC reports sub payments at year end (1099s). A missing W-9 stops the payment, not the work.
Lien waiver types: conditional progress (signed with the pay app, valid only once paid), unconditional progress (after the check clears), conditional final and unconditional final.
Some states prescribe statutory waiver forms, Texas among them. Use the GC's forms, and never state a legal requirement to anyone.
goesWrong: Certificates arrive with missing wording, wrong limits or the wrong entity name, and the loop starts again
Policies expire mid-project, so the chase has to start about 30 days ahead
A sub signs the wrong waiver type, or for $48,000 when $50,000 is owed, or three days late, and the owner holds the GC's whole payment

Worked example: an electrician owed $50,000 for September signs a conditional progress waiver in early October; the GC bundles it with every other sub's waiver and its own pay app; the owner releases payment; the GC pays the electrician; the electrician signs an unconditional progress waiver, collected with the next cycle; final versions come at the end of the job

primer.why: GCs are paid monthly for the percentage of work complete, not when the building is done, and the pay application is that monthly package. The GC bills the owner, and every sub bills the GC with its own pay app, so the GC rolls sub pay apps up and pays subs after it is paid. Retainage, commonly 5 to 10 percent but set by contract, is held back both ways until the job is complete. If a pay app is late or rejected, or a waiver is missing, the GC's cash slips while payroll and materials still come due, and subs get paid late.
terms: Schedule of values: the line-item breakdown of the contract price, agreed with the owner at the start. The skeleton of every pay app.
Percent complete per line: the PM's or superintendent's judgment of what is built. Never the VA's.
Stored materials: bought but not yet installed, sometimes billable with documentation.
Approved change orders are added to the contract and the SOV so they can be billed.
Backup: sub pay apps, lien waivers, and sometimes invoices and certified payroll, attached to support the numbers.
G702 is the summary cover sheet; G703 is the continuation sheet with the line items.
Pay-when-paid and pay-if-paid clauses tie a sub's payment to the owner paying the GC. Enforceability varies by state and wording, so never explain their legal effect.
goesWrong: The monthly crunch: numbers, backup and waivers all gathered at the deadline
An Excel pay app with a broken formula or an out-of-date SOV, caught by the owner's side and returned, so payment slides by weeks
Retainage running totals per line and per sub drift out of sync
An approved change order never reaches the pay app and is never billed: lost margin for a business running at 5 to 15 percent
Unpaid owner invoices pile up because nobody is assigned to follow up consistently

primer.why: RFIs, submittals and change orders are formal written processes because informal agreements on site are how disputes and unpaid work happen. Daily logs and photos are the evidence months later in a delay claim, a dispute over extra work or an insurance claim.
terms: RFI: GC to architect. 'Your plans are unclear, what do you mean?' Logged with a number and date and tracked until answered.

Submittal: GC to architect. 'Here is the exact product I plan to use, do you approve?' Approved, approved with comments, or rejected. A project can have hundreds, each with a review window and long-lead items.
Change order: GC and owner. 'We are changing the deal, here is the new price and schedule.' Work should not proceed on a change without written approval.
Daily log: weather, who was on site, what work happened, deliveries, visitors, delays and safety events.
Permits and inspections vary by jurisdiction. Ask how each city or county works rather than assume.
goesWrong: Unanswered RFIs hold up work, and the log's dates decide delay claims
A late or rejected submittal delays the schedule by weeks
Change logs fall behind, and approved changes are missed on the next pay app
PMs write logs late or from memory; photos sit unsorted on phones and personal cloud accounts with no names or dates

How do you track retainage on both sides, owed to you and owed to subs?
Has an approved change order ever fallen through the cracks and gone unbilled?
On average, how long does it take from submitting a pay app to getting paid?
Who follows up on late owner payments, and how consistently?
Has cash flow ever limited the jobs you could take on?
How do you track RFIs, submittals and change orders today: software, spreadsheet, or email?
Who follows up when the architect is slow to respond?
Who writes your daily logs, and how current do they stay?
If you had to find a specific photo from three months ago, how long would it take?
How do you invite subs to bid, and how do you know who is actually bidding?
How long does it take to level bids and put together a proposal?
Do you track win and loss by bid, and does anyone follow up after you submit?
What software do you run projects and accounting in?
Where does information get typed twice?
Where does your next job come from, and who keeps those relationships warm?
Do you track bid opportunities and past clients in one place?

pivot.line: Their person owns the decisions. The VA owns the follow-through.
pivot.intro: “I already have someone who does that” rarely ends the conversation. It means the work has an owner, not that it gets done on time, every time, without pulling a busy person off higher-value work. Find the gap around the person they have and offer to fill it next to them.
moves: Agree, don't defend. “Good, that tells me it matters to you.”
Get specific. “Who handles it, and what does a normal month look like?”
Find the edge. Listen for: late, backlog, “when someone gets to it”, one person doing too much, nobody covering when they're out, an expensive person doing low-value work.
Offer the smallest add-on. One task, two weeks, alongside their person. Never “instead of”.
edgeQuestions: What part of that do you wish happened faster?
When that person is out for a week, what happens to it?
What does that person have to put off to get it done?
Is anything done late, or only when someone has time?
If your PM got five hours a week back, what would they do with it?
example: GC: “My office manager already does that.”
You: “Good, that tells me it matters. Who follows up when an owner is 60 days late?”
GC: “Honestly, nobody. Whenever she gets to it.”
You: “That's the gap. We wouldn't replace her. We'd take the chasing so she can keep the books clean. Could we try one task for two weeks?”

byWhoHasIt.says: My office manager or bookkeeper does that.
byWhoHasIt.hides: One person covering AP, AR, payroll and compliance. Chasing and follow-up slip first because they are repetitive and awkward.
byWhoHasIt.ask: Who follows up when an owner is 60 days late on a payment?
byWhoHasIt.add: Unpaid invoice follow-up and the aging report; COI and W-9 chasing. The bookkeeper keeps the books and approvals.

byWhoHasIt.says: My PM or coordinator handles RFIs, submittals and change orders.
byWhoHasIt.hides: The PM's time going to logs and chasing instead of running the job.
byWhoHasIt.ask: How current is your submittal log right now, and who chases the architect when a review is late?
byWhoHasIt.add: Submittal, RFI and change order logs, permits tracking. The PM keeps drafting, pricing and decisions.

byWhoHasIt.hides: Bid week spent on logistics (chasing quotes, formatting) instead of pricing.
byWhoHasIt.ask: How much of bid week goes to chasing sub quotes and assembling the package?
byWhoHasIt.add: Quote chasing, proposal assembly, bid prep. The estimator keeps pricing and scope.

byWhoHasIt.says: I do it myself, or a family member helps.
byWhoHasIt.hides: The owner is head of sales and head firefighter, so inbox, calendar and follow-ups slip.
byWhoHasIt.ask: What's the one thing you keep putting off?
byWhoHasIt.add: Owner inbox and calendar, scheduling subs and site visits, proposal follow-up.

byWhoHasIt.says: We have software for that (Procore, Buildertrend, QuickBooks).
byWhoHasIt.hides: Software stores information. It doesn't chase people, fill itself in or reconcile. Someone still keys things in and nudges.
byWhoHasIt.ask: Who keeps it updated, and where do people still use email or spreadsheets?
byWhoHasIt.add: Keeping it current, chasing, and entering once across systems, inside the access the GC grants.

byWhoHasIt.says: My outside bookkeeper or CPA handles that.
byWhoHasIt.hides: They work in monthly or quarterly batches, not day-to-day follow-up.
byWhoHasIt.ask: Who handles it between their visits?
byWhoHasIt.add: Day-to-day tracking and invoice follow-up, so the outside bookkeeper gets clean information.

byWhoHasIt.says: We already have a VA or an offshore team.
byWhoHasIt.hides: Don't assume what's wrong. Gaps in tasks, hours or construction know-how.
byWhoHasIt.ask: What do they cover, what hours, and what's not getting covered?
byWhoHasIt.add: Lean on what is settled: a dedicated, construction-trained, English-fluent assistant on the client's hours, in accounts the client owns.

byWhoHasIt.ask: When your workload spikes, or that person leaves, what's the plan?
byWhoHasIt.add: Leave the door open and ask whether anyone they know is stretched thin. Don't force it.

guardrails: Say “takes repeat work off their plate”, not “replaces your person”.
Quote the website's plans and terms. Do not promise a start date or an assistant count that isn't settled; use “I'll confirm and get back to you by [day]”.
Do not claim system access or security details beyond the access catalog and the confidentiality agreement.
Do not state legal requirements: waiver forms, pay-when-paid, licensing. Ask what forms they use and who owns the process.
Everything about their setup is a question until they confirm it.
Dollar figures, percentages and counts in the primers are typical ranges for illustration, never facts about a prospect.
openItems: Vendor setup in the GC's accounting system: offer it by name, or keep it inside QuickBooks data entry? Flagged in the Deep Dive review as a question of whether we can do it at all.
W-9 and taxpayer-ID handling: the VA rule here is that they stay in the GC's systems. Write the client-facing answer, since prospects ask before they book.
Licenses and registrations: which states and municipalities require what for the trades we serve. Build the matrix before promising license tracking on public work.
Capacity: submittals on a large job, and daily logs plus photos across several jobs, can each be a full-time load. Set expectations with the VA and the GC on volume before handing either off.
Which client systems the team may work in securely is answered by the access catalog; confirm it with each client at kickoff and log it in the register.
Percent complete and the SOV are sometimes kept by the GC's PM. Where a PM exists, find the gap (the crunch, the backup, the waivers) rather than offering to take the pay app itself.
